questions.stem: An off-duty nurse stops at a highway crash, checks the driver's breathing and holds pressure on a bleeding scalp wound until paramedics arrive. The nurse is not paid and stays within first-aid skills. What protects the nurse legally?

options.text: A Good Samaritan law, if care is within training and not grossly negligent
The employer's malpractice policy, because the nurse holds an active license
The nurse's personal liability policy bought for work
The injured driver's implied consent to emergency treatment

rationale.correct: Good Samaritan laws protect good-faith emergency care given without pay and within the person's training.

perOption.a: Good Samaritan laws protect people who give emergency help in good faith, without payment, within their training.
perOption.b: Employer policies usually cover only work done for the employer.
perOption.c: A personal policy may help, but Good Samaritan laws are the main protection here.
perOption.d: Implied consent allows treatment to begin, but it is not protection from liability.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The emergency department nurse is reviewing the day's cases with a new graduate. Which situations must be reported to the proper authorities by law in most states? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client treated for a gunshot wound to the thigh
Suspected neglect of an adult with dementia by a caregiver
A child with a new diagnosis of measles
A positive syphilis test in a pregnant client
A client's decision to refuse a recommended surgery
A client's seasonal allergies needing a prescription

rationale.correct: Mandatory reports include certain injuries, abuse and neglect, and listed communicable diseases.

perOption.a: Most states require reporting gunshot and stab wounds.
perOption.b: Nurses are mandated reporters of elder and dependent-adult abuse and neglect.
perOption.c: Measles is a reportable communicable disease.
perOption.d: Syphilis is a reportable disease.
perOption.e: Refusal is the client's right and is not reportable.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A confused client keeps trying to climb out of bed at night. Frustrated, a nurse says to the client, "If you get up one more time, I'm going to tie you to the bed." The nurse does not touch the client. Which tort does this describe?

options.text: Assault
Battery
False imprisonment
Defamation

rationale.correct: Assault is a threat of harmful contact; battery is unwanted touching; false imprisonment is unlawful restraint.

perOption.a: Assault is a threat that makes a person fear harmful or offensive contact.
perOption.b: Battery is actual touching without consent; no contact happened.
perOption.c: False imprisonment requires actual restraint of movement.
perOption.d: Defamation is a false statement that harms someone's reputation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A competent woman admitted voluntarily for chest pain says she is going home. Staff lock the unit door and tell her she cannot leave until the cardiologist sees her tomorrow. No legal hold has been placed. Which tort does this describe?

options.text: False imprisonment
Negligence
Assault
Abandonment

rationale.correct: A competent client may leave unless a lawful hold applies; locking her in is false imprisonment.

perOption.a: Unlawfully restricting a competent person's movement is false imprisonment.
perOption.b: Negligence is failing to meet the standard of care, causing harm.
perOption.c: Assault is a threat of harmful contact.
perOption.d: Abandonment is ending care without a proper handoff.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A new graduate asks where the legal limits of an RN's practice are set. Which document defines the legal scope of practice for registered nurses in a state?

options.text: The state's nurse practice act
The hospital's policy manual
The ANA Code of Ethics
The unit's procedure book

rationale.correct: The nurse practice act sets the legal scope of nursing practice; facility policy can only be the same or narrower.

perOption.a: Each state's nurse practice act defines scope of practice and licensure.
perOption.b: Facility policies cannot expand legal scope.
perOption.c: The Code is an ethical guide, not law.
perOption.d: Procedures describe how, not the legal scope.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the source of scope of practice.

questions.stem: A nurse sees that a coworker has posted a photo of a client's unusual wound on a private social media account, with the caption "Wild night on 4 West!" The client's face is not shown. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave it alone, since the client's face cannot be seen
Report it according to the facility's social media policy
Comment on the post asking the coworker to blur the wound
Message the coworker privately and keep it between the two of them

rationale.correct: Never post client information or images on social media; report breaches through policy.

perOption.a: The unit, date and wound can still identify the client, and posting breaches privacy.
perOption.b: Posting client images without consent violates privacy and professional standards and must be reported.
perOption.c: Engaging publicly spreads the post further and does not fix the breach.
perOption.d: A privacy breach must be reported, not handled informally.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a social media privacy breach.

questions.stem: A risk manager is reviewing four events. Which event shows all four elements of malpractice: duty, breach, causation and harm?

options.text: A nurse forgot to chart a normal blood pressure, and the client was discharged well
A nurse ignored a falling blood pressure, and the client had a stroke from bleeding
A client fell and broke a hip even though every fall precaution in the plan was in place
A nurse gave an antibiotic 90 minutes late, and the client had no ill effects

rationale.correct: Malpractice requires all four elements: a duty, a breach of the standard of care, causation and damages.

perOption.a: There was a breach of documentation standards, but no harm resulted.
perOption.b: The nurse had a duty, breached the standard, and the breach caused harm.
perOption.c: Harm occurred, but there was no breach of the standard of care.
perOption.d: There was a breach, but no harm resulted.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with no insurance arrives at a private hospital's emergency department in active labor, with contractions every 3 minutes. The registration clerk asks whether the client should be sent to the county hospital 20 miles away. What does the law require?

options.text: Transfer to the county hospital once the client's insurance status is confirmed
A medical screening exam and stabilizing care, whatever the client can pay
Payment or a payment plan before anything other than a fetal heart check
Treatment if the on-call obstetrician agrees to accept the client

rationale.correct: EMTALA requires emergency screening and stabilizing treatment, including for active labor, regardless of ability to pay.

perOption.a: Transfer before screening and stabilization violates EMTALA.
perOption.b: EMTALA requires screening and stabilization, including delivery in active labor, for anyone who comes to the ED.
perOption.c: Asking about payment cannot delay screening or stabilization.
perOption.d: The duty to screen and stabilize does not depend on a physician agreeing.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The unit's ethics resource nurse is discussing four situations with staff. For each situation, choose the ethical principle that is most at stake.

rows.text: A competent client refuses dialysis after hearing the risks
Deciding which of two clients gets the last ICU bed
Holding a sedative that would lower a client's already dangerous blood pressure
Spending extra time helping a frightened client understand the plan

rationale.correct: Autonomy is self-determination, beneficence is doing good, justice is fairness, and nonmaleficence is avoiding harm.

perOption.r1:c1: The client's right to decide is at stake.
perOption.r1:c2: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r1:c3: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r1:c4: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r2:c1: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r2:c2: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r2:c3: Fair distribution of scarce resources is at stake.
perOption.r2:c4: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r3:c1: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r3:c2: Related, but the focus is avoiding harm.
perOption.r3:c3: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r4:c1: Related, but the focus is doing good.
perOption.r4:c2: Acting for the client's benefit is at stake.
perOption.r4:c3: This is not the main issue.
perOption.r4:c4: This is not the main issue.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client dying of pancreatic cancer receives increasing doses of IV morphine for severe pain. The client's son says, "I'm afraid the morphine will make him die sooner." The client's pain is now controlled. Which ethical principle supports continuing to give the morphine for pain?

options.text: The principle of double effect
The principle of paternalism
The principle of fidelity
The principle of veracity

rationale.correct: Double effect: when the intent is pain relief, not hastening death, giving the opioid is ethical.

perOption.a: An act meant to relieve suffering is ethical even if a foreseen, unintended effect follows.
perOption.b: Paternalism is overriding a client's wishes for their own good, which is not happening here.
perOption.c: Fidelity is keeping promises.
perOption.d: Veracity is truth-telling.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the principle of double effect.

questions.stem: A nurse is scheduled to assist with a procedure next week that conflicts with the nurse's deeply held personal beliefs. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client at the bedside that the nurse will not take part
Tell the manager in advance so the client's care is safely reassigned
Leave the unit when the procedure starts without telling anyone
Share the nurse's concerns with the client so the client can reconsider

rationale.correct: Conscientious objection requires advance notice and a safe transfer of care, without judging the client.

perOption.a: Refusing in front of the client is unprofessional and distressing.
perOption.b: Conscientious objection is acceptable when it is raised early and care is not abandoned.
perOption.c: Walking away from assigned care is abandonment.
perOption.d: This imposes the nurse's values on the client.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who is deaf and uses American Sign Language (ASL) needs teaching before a cardiac catheterization this afternoon. The client's hearing teenage daughter is visiting. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Write the key teaching points in English for the client to read
Arrange a qualified ASL interpreter, in person or by video
Ask the daughter to sign the teaching, since she knows the client well
Face the client and speak slowly so the client can lip-read

rationale.correct: Use qualified sign language interpreters, in person or by video, for clients who are deaf.

perOption.a: Many ASL users are not fluent readers of English, so written notes may not work.
perOption.b: Clients are entitled to effective communication through a qualified interpreter.
perOption.c: Family interpreters may be inaccurate and breach privacy, and a child should not interpret.
perOption.d: Lip-reading catches only part of speech and is not reliable for teaching.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A woman scheduled for a mastectomy tomorrow tells the nurse, "The surgeon said this is my only option, but my friend had a lumpectomy and radiation. I wanted to ask about that, but the surgeon was in a hurry." The consent form has not been signed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the client that the surgeon has chosen the best option for her
Tell the surgeon the client wants to discuss alternatives before consenting
Explain the differences between mastectomy and lumpectomy to the client
Postpone tomorrow's surgery on the schedule until the client is completely sure

rationale.correct: Nurses advocate by making sure the provider answers the client's questions about alternatives before consent.

perOption.a: This dismisses the client's right to information about alternatives.
perOption.b: Advocacy means making sure the client gets the information needed for an informed choice.
perOption.c: The surgeon explains options and alternatives as part of informed consent.
perOption.d: Rescheduling is not the nurse's decision.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old comes to a clinic alone, reports painful urination and a discharge, and asks to be tested and treated for a sexually transmitted infection without the parents being told. What applies in most states?

options.text: The adolescent can consent to STI testing and treatment
A parent signs the consent before testing is done
The nurse must notify a parent once a test is positive
Testing can be done, but treatment waits for a parent

rationale.correct: Minors can consent to some services, such as STI care, contraception and substance use treatment, depending on state law.

perOption.a: Most states allow minors to consent to STI care so they are not deterred from getting it.
perOption.b: STI care is one of the common exceptions to parental consent.
perOption.c: Confidentiality applies to care the minor consented to.
perOption.d: The exception covers both testing and treatment.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is invited to join a clinical trial of a new medication and has read the consent document. Which statement by the client shows understanding of research consent?

options.text: "Once I sign, I have to stay in the study until it ends."
"I can leave the study whenever I want and still get my usual care."
"My doctor will look after me less carefully if I say no."
"The researchers will tell me the risks if something goes wrong."

rationale.correct: Research consent is voluntary and informed, and it can be withdrawn at any time without affecting usual care.

perOption.a: Participants may withdraw at any time.
perOption.b: Participation is voluntary, and withdrawing cannot affect usual care.
perOption.c: Refusing to take part cannot affect the client's care.
perOption.d: Known risks must be explained before consent.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 91-year-old nursing home resident with a valid POLST form stating "Do not attempt resuscitation; comfort measures only" is found not breathing and without a pulse. The resident's daughter, who has just arrived, shouts, "Do something! Start CPR!" What should the nurse do?

options.text: Start CPR, because the family member at the bedside has asked for it
Follow the POLST order, notify the provider and support the daughter
Call the facility's lawyer for advice before doing anything else
Start CPR while another nurse looks for the resident's other children

rationale.correct: Honor a valid POLST or advance directive, and support grieving family members.

perOption.a: The resident's documented wishes and the POLST order take priority.
perOption.b: A POLST is a medical order reflecting the resident's wishes and is honored.
perOption.c: This delays care and is not needed for a valid order.
perOption.d: Starting CPR violates the order, whoever else is reached.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An unconscious client on a ventilator after a cardiac arrest has no advance directive and no named health care agent. The client's two adult children disagree: one wants all treatment continued, the other says their parent would never want this. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the wishes of the older child, who is the legal next of kin
Ask for an ethics consultation and a family meeting with the team
Ask the provider to begin withdrawing the ventilator today
Ask the client's relatives to vote on what should happen

rationale.correct: Ethics committees help resolve conflicts between surrogates by focusing on what the client would have wanted.

perOption.a: Both adult children usually have equal standing; age alone does not decide.
perOption.b: An ethics consultation and a team meeting help the family reach a decision based on the client's values.
perOption.c: Treatment is not withdrawn without a proper decision process.
perOption.d: A vote is not an accepted way to make surrogate decisions.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to family conflict about care.

questions.stem: A nurse's husband is admitted to another unit in the same hospital. The nurse wants to see his morning lab results and has access to the electronic health record. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Look up the results, because spouses share medical information
Ask the husband or his care team for them, as any visitor would
Look up the results if the husband gives verbal permission first
Look up the results but avoid sharing them with any coworkers

rationale.correct: Use record access only for your assigned work (the minimum necessary standard), even for family members.

perOption.a: Being a spouse does not create a work-related reason to open the record.
perOption.b: Access is limited to records needed for the nurse's job; family information comes through the usual channels.
perOption.c: Permission to share does not authorize the nurse to use work access.
perOption.d: Unauthorized access is a violation even if nothing is shared.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During the evening shift, the electronic health record and the medication scanning system go down without warning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop giving medications until the system is working
Use the facility's downtime procedures and forms
Write notes on scrap paper and throw them out later
Postpone all charting until the end of the shift

rationale.correct: Know and use the facility's downtime procedures for documentation and medication administration.

perOption.a: Care continues during downtime.
perOption.b: Downtime procedures keep care and documentation safe.
perOption.c: Records must be kept properly.
perOption.d: Timely documentation still matters.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse manager is auditing documentation in the electronic health record. Which practice found in the audit is unsafe?

options.text: Copying the last shift's assessment forward without reassessing
Documenting a client's refusal of care along with the client's own words
Charting a dressing change within 30 minutes of finishing it
Logging off the workstation before walking away from it

rationale.correct: Document only what you assessed and did; avoid copy-forward and copy-and-paste errors.

perOption.a: Copy-forward can record findings that are no longer true and hide changes.
perOption.b: Recording refusals and the client's words is correct.
perOption.c: Timely documentation is correct.
perOption.d: Logging off protects client information.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse scans a dose of clarithromycin for a client who takes simvastatin, and the electronic health record shows a drug interaction alert. The unit has many alerts each day. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Override the alert, since most alerts on the unit are not significant
Read the alert and ask the pharmacist or provider before giving it
Give half of the clarithromycin dose and recheck the alert later
Ask the informatics team to turn off interaction alerts for the unit

rationale.correct: Respond to clinical decision support alerts by reading them and checking with the pharmacist or provider, not by habitually overriding.

perOption.a: Alert fatigue causes errors; this interaction can cause serious muscle injury.
perOption.b: The alert may show a real risk that needs a change in therapy.
perOption.c: Changing the dose is outside the nurse's scope.
perOption.d: Turning off alerts removes a safety feature.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse is holding a telehealth follow-up visit from home with a client recovering from pneumonia. Which action best protects the client's privacy?

options.text: Using a secure, approved platform in a private room
Using a personal social media video call app
Holding the visit at a quiet table in a coffee shop
Recording the visit on a personal phone for notes

rationale.correct: Telehealth privacy requires a secure, approved platform and a private setting.

perOption.a: Telehealth must use secure platforms and private spaces.
perOption.b: Social media apps are not secure for health care.
perOption.c: Others can overhear.
perOption.d: Personal devices are not secure.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client who takes nine medications, including a sleeping pill, a diuretic and two blood pressure drugs, has had three falls and frequent dizziness when standing at home this month. Which team member is most helpful for a medication review?

options.text: Pharmacist
Physical therapist
Dietitian
Case manager

rationale.correct: Pharmacists review medication lists for interactions and drugs that raise fall risk in older adults.

perOption.a: Pharmacists find interactions, duplications and drugs that raise fall risk.
perOption.b: PT helps with strength and balance, but does not review medications.
perOption.c: A dietitian does not review medications.
perOption.d: A case manager coordinates services, not medication review.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client recovering from a right-sided stroke has left-sided weakness and wants to dress and bathe without help before going home. Swallowing and speech are normal, and the client walks with a cane. Which referral is most appropriate?

options.text: Occupational therapy
Speech-language pathology
Physical therapy
Case management

rationale.correct: Occupational therapy focuses on activities of daily living such as dressing and bathing.

perOption.a: OT helps clients relearn activities of daily living with adaptive techniques and equipment.
perOption.b: Swallowing and speech are normal.
perOption.c: PT focuses on walking and mobility; dressing and bathing are OT's focus.
perOption.d: A case manager coordinates services but does not train ADLs.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is handing off a client who had a hip replacement this morning to the night nurse using the I-PASS format. Place the parts of the handoff in order, from first to last.

items.text: Action list: what must be done and by when
Patient summary: diagnosis, events and plan
Synthesis by receiver: the receiving nurse summarizes

rationale.correct: I-PASS: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness, Synthesis by receiver.

perOption.a: This tells the receiver how worried to be.
perOption.b: This gives the context.
perOption.c: This makes tasks clear.
perOption.d: This covers what could go wrong and what to do.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: During a cardiac arrest, the code team leader says, "Give epinephrine 1 mg IV push." The nurse at the medication cart has the drug ready. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it straight away without speaking, to save time
Repeat the order back, give it and say when it is in
Wait for the order to be written before giving it
Ask the recorder to confirm the dose before giving it

rationale.correct: Closed-loop communication: repeat the order back, carry it out, then confirm it is done.

perOption.a: Closed-loop communication prevents errors in a noisy room.
perOption.b: Closed-loop communication confirms each order and its completion.
perOption.c: Verbal orders are used during emergencies.
perOption.d: The leader gave the order; repeating it back to the leader confirms it.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a colleague's notes for a client 2 days after a hip replacement before co-signing the shift summary. Highlight the entries that are inappropriate.

segments.text: Client resting quietly, respirations 16, SpO2 96% on room air.
Client is being difficult and lazy about walking.
Client found sitting on the floor beside the bed; denies pain; provider notified at 1007.
Dr. Lee made an error with the order again.

rationale.correct: Document facts objectively; leave out opinions, blame and references to incident reports.

perOption.s6: Incident reports are not mentioned in the medical record.
perOption.s10: Blaming statements do not belong in the record.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with heart failure who left school at age 14 is going home on four new medications. The nurse suspects the client has low health literacy. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use plain language and avoid medical terms
Ask the client to explain the plan back in their own words
Focus on the two or three most important points
Use pictures, pill charts or demonstrations
Give the full set of printed leaflets to read at home
Ask "Do you understand?" and move on if the client says yes

rationale.correct: Health literacy strategies: plain language, teach-back, a few key points and visual aids.

perOption.a: Plain language improves understanding.
perOption.b: Teach-back confirms understanding.
perOption.c: Key messages are remembered better.
perOption.d: Visual aids help understanding.
perOption.e: Large amounts of print overwhelm the client.
perOption.f: Clients may say yes without understanding.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach clients with low health literacy.

questions.stem: A nurse with a multistate license whose primary residence is in one Nurse Licensure Compact state accepts a travel position in another compact state. What is true?

options.text: The nurse needs a new license from the second state before starting work
The nurse may work there under the multistate license and local law
The nurse may now practice in any state or any country without restriction
The nurse gives up the home-state license to work in the other state

rationale.correct: The Nurse Licensure Compact lets nurses practice across member states, following the practice laws where the client is located.

perOption.a: The compact lets the nurse work in other member states on the multistate license.
perOption.b: The Nurse Licensure Compact allows this, and the nurse follows the practice laws of the state where the client is.
perOption.c: The compact covers member states only.
perOption.d: The home-state license is what allows multistate practice.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A nurse has reported dangerous staffing levels to the unit manager and the director of nursing several times in writing over 3 months, with no change. Two clients have fallen. The nurse is now considering reporting to the state health department. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Good-faith reports of unsafe conditions are often protected by whistleblower laws
The nurse can be fired for any report made outside of the organization
The nurse should post the details on social media to get public attention
The nurse should stay silent to protect the facility's reputation in the community

rationale.correct: Use internal channels first; whistleblower protections support good-faith reporting to outside agencies when internal reports fail.

perOption.a: Many state and federal laws protect nurses who report unsafe conditions in good faith after using internal channels.
perOption.b: Whistleblower protections exist in many states.
perOption.c: Social media is not an appropriate channel and may breach privacy.
perOption.d: Client safety comes before the facility's reputation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
